title: Tide and Postcard
premise: Rafael Ashgrove, once the most sought-after wedding planner on the coast, now runs her business on autopilot after a betrayal she has never named aloud. When a community library's anonymous pen-pal program misfiles its cards, she begins exchanging letters with Julian Vane, the rival planner who destroyed her career a decade ago—neither knowing who holds the other's postcard. As their correspondence deepens into honesty neither can afford in person, Rafael discovers Julian took the fall for someone else, and that the sentence she rehearsed for ten years—I forgive you, and I was wrong too—must be spoken before his failing eyesight, and the demolition of the seaside chapel where it all began, erase the chance forever.
about_author: Paloma Dravenmoor spent seven years coordinating weddings in coastal towns before trading clipboards for manuscripts, and she still keeps a drawer of unsent letters as research. She writes love stories about people who are fluent in everyone else's happiness except their own.

chapters.title: The Last Bouquet
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She executes a flawless society wedding while feeling nothing, then quietly declines a client who asks her to 'make us believe again.' At home she rereads one old postcard from a decade ago. Emotional beat: hollow competence; the reader sees the wound before understanding it.

chapters.title: Dead Letters Desk
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. The librarian conscripts Julian, now semi-retired and losing his sight, into the anonymous pen-pal program to 'get him out of himself.' He writes a guarded first letter about tides. Beat: reluctant tenderness; he signs only 'J.'

chapters.title: Mismatched Cards
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. A filing error at the library pairs her card with Julian's letter. Not recognizing the handwriting through the typewritten copy, she answers with sarcasm about the wedding industry. Beat: sparks through paper; dramatic irony established.

chapters.title: Enemies, Anonymously
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Their letters sharpen into a duel—he defends marriage, she dismantles it—yet both catch themselves smiling at the mail slot. Meanwhile they clash in person over a shared venue booking. Beat: enemies on two tracks, unaware they're allies on one.

chapters.title: What the Tide Took
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Flashback chapter: the ruined wedding ten years ago, the forged vendor contract, the chapel where she was supposed to be married herself. We learn why she blames Julian. Beat: grief given architecture; sympathy tilts toward her anger.

chapters.title: The Other Signature
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian rereads his own confession draft—the truth about who actually forged the contract—and burns it instead of sending it. His vision blurs mid-sentence. Beat: cowardice and urgency braided together; the clock starts ticking.

chapters.title: Postcards from the Chapel
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She visits the condemned seaside chapel to salvage fixtures before demolition and finds Julian there doing the same. They argue, almost connect, and part without either admitting the pen-pal letters exist. Beat: proximity without recognition; ache of near-miss.

chapters.title: Ink Under the Skin
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The anonymous letters turn vulnerable: Rafael confesses (without names) that she was left at the altar; Julian confesses he let a lie stand to protect someone. Each recognizes the other's pain but not the person. Beat: intimacy outpacing identity.

chapters.title: The Client Who Knew
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. A bride-to-be turns out to be the daughter of Marisol Vane—Julian's late wife—and mentions 'Uncle Julian' lost his sight and his reputation in the same year. Rafael pieces together that J might be Julian Vane. Beat: dread blooming; she stops answering.

chapters.title: Silence by Return Post
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian waits for a reply that doesn't come, and dictates a final honest letter to the librarian, asking her to hold it 'until I'm brave.' His sight fails enough that he can no longer read Rafael's earlier letters unaided. Beat: loss compounding; regret made physical.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The chapel's demolition moves up two weeks. Rafael, hired to plan the farewell event on the site, must work alongside Julian daily while withholding what she suspects. Beat: tension of double life; every kindness feels like betrayal.

chapters.title: Marisol's Letters
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian sorts Marisol's belongings and finds her own unsent letter revealing she asked him to take the blame for the forgery—she did it to save them financially, and died before confessing. Beat: the twist lands; his decade of silence reframed as devotion, not villainy.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The librarian, torn by confidentiality, lets slip that the silent correspondent is going blind. Rafael, shaken, offers to read Julian's archived letters aloud at the chapel event—unknowingly volunteering to hear her own words in his voice. Beat: trap of her own compassion.

chapters.title: The Voice in the Paper
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Rehearsing the reading, Rafael recognizes a phrase from her own letter in Julian's stack. She confirms the pen-pal is Julian and nearly walks away—then reads his confession-to-a-stranger about the woman he wronged, and hears the guilt beneath it. Beat: recognition; fury and longing collide.

chapters.title: Rehearsed for a Decade
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She drafts and destroys a dozen confrontations, finally writing the sentence she's carried ten years onto a postcard addressed to no one. Her sister forces her to admit she stopped believing in weddings the day she stopped believing she deserved one. Beat: interior climax; the theme of inheritance—of blame—surfacing.

chapters.title: Farewell to the Chapel
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. At the farewell event, Julian gives a speech about the chapel and publicly takes responsibility for the old scandal—then goes further and names Marisol as the true author, freeing the dead and damning himself. Beat: sacrifice; the crowd's gasp mirrors Rafael's.

chapters.title: Say It Before the Tide Does
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Climax. As demolition equipment idles outside, Rafael finds Julian alone in the chapel and speaks the rehearsed sentence—I forgive you, and I was wrong too—then shows him the pen-pal letters, revealing who he's been writing all along. Beat: catharsis; identity and forgiveness arrive together.

chapters.title: What He Couldn't Read
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian, unable to see her face clearly, asks her to read her own letters aloud. Hearing a decade of his damage answered line by line, he weeps for the first time since Marisol's death. Beat: vulnerability rewarded; sight vs. insight inverted.

chapters.title: One Wedding, Believed In
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Epilogue-in-motion: Rafael agrees to plan one final wedding—not a client's, but a small ceremony in the half-demolished chapel garden, hers and Julian's, witnessed by the librarian and the town. Beat: restoration; the skeptic plans the wedding she once couldn't imagine.

chapters.title: Vows in Large Print
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. The wedding day. Julian recites vows printed in letters large enough for him to see, and Rafael guides his hand to sign the register. The tide turns below the cliffs on cue. Beat: joy earned; memory honored rather than escaped.

chapters.title: Return to Sender
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Weeks later, Rafael mails one last postcard to the dead-letter desk—an answer to Marisol's unsent letter, thanking her and letting the guilt go. She reopens her business under a new name: Ashgrove & Vane. Beat: inheritance transformed; the past put gently down.

chapters.title: Tide and Postcard
chapters.summary: Closing dual POV, brief alternating paragraphs. On the first anniversary, they walk the new shoreline path where the chapel stood, mailing a postcard to themselves so the future will have proof. Final line echoes the rehearsed sentence, now spoken easily. Beat: quiet resolution; love kept in the present tense.
